title: A TRRIP Down Memory Lane: Temperature-Based Re-Reference Interval Prediction For Instruction Caching
problem: Modern mobile CPU workloads (interpreters, JIT compilers, UI frameworks) have large instruction footprints with long reuse distances that defeat hardware-only cache replacement policies, causing persistent L2 instruction cache miss stalls even after PGO code layout optimization.
method: TRRIP is a compiler-OS-hardware co-design cache replacement policy. The LLVM PGO compiler classifies basic blocks as hot/warm/cold by execution frequency and places them in separate ELF sections (.text.hot, .text.warm, .text.cold). The OS loader reads these ELF headers and encodes temperature (2 bits) into existing ARM PBHA bits in page table entries (PTEs), requiring no ISA changes. The MMU transfers temperature bits with every memory request to the L2 cache. The hardware replacement policy extends RRIP: hot instruction lines are inserted at Immediate re-reference priority (RRPV=0), warm lines at Near (RRPV=1), cold/data lines at Intermediate (RRPV=2) per the existing RRIP eviction scan. The variant TRRIP-2 additionally decelerates RRPV promotion for non-hot hits. No additional on-chip storage is required beyond existing PTE bits.

title: Lumos: Efficient Performance Modeling and Estimation for Large-Scale LLM Training
problem: Existing performance models for distributed LLM training fail to accurately capture complex inter-stream dependencies (computation-communication overlap), leading to large prediction errors (dPRO averages 14% error) and preventing reliable what-if analysis for configuration exploration.
method: Lumos: a trace-driven performance modeling and estimation toolkit. Uses PyTorch Kineto profiler (only ~10 lines of hook code) to collect CPU operator traces, CUDA runtime events, and GPU kernel traces. Constructs a task-level execution graph with four dependency types: CPU-to-CPU (intra/inter-thread via cudaLaunchKernel), CPU-to-GPU (correlation IDs), GPU-to-CPU (cudaStreamSync), GPU-to-GPU (intra/inter-stream via cudaEventRecord/cudaStreamWaitEvent). Graph manipulation supports adjusting data parallelism (update communication times), pipeline parallelism (repartition layers, insert communication tasks, update schedule), and model architecture (adjust tensor dimensions for GEMM kernels, duplicate layers). Simulation runs a dependency-respecting event-driven scheduler producing replayed traces.

title: LLMulator: Generalizable Cost Modeling for Dataflow Accelerators with Input-Adaptive Control Flow
problem: Existing performance prediction methods for dataflow-based accelerators (TPUs, NPUs, FPGAs) fail to generalize across three dimensions: unseen applications with extreme loop scales (errors exceeding 40%), input-dependent control flows where branch probabilities shift at runtime (errors up to 60%), and diverse hardware architectures with varying memory delays and loop mapping primitives. No prior method unifies all three generalization axes.
method: LLMulator uses a pre-trained LLM (LLaMA-3.2-1B fine-tuned via LoRA) as the backbone for cost prediction with three novel mechanisms: (1) Progressive numeric encoding that tokenizes each decimal digit independently and uses categorical cross-entropy rather than regression to predict performance as digit-wise classification with beam-search error correction, enabling range-agnostic estimates; (2) Dynamic Prediction Calibration (DPC) using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)-style reinforcement learning with a replay buffer, where the model is updated online from Verilator simulation feedback to adapt to runtime input variations in loop bounds and control-flow branching; (3) A progressive dataset synthesizer that generates multi-level training data via AST-based generation, dataflow-specific loop-tree mutation, and LLM-based augmentation, then formats data with intermediate RTL reasoning chains (via SiliconCompiler and OpenROAD) to teach the model compilation-level reasoning.

title: MOAT: Securely Mitigating Rowhammer with Per-Row Activation Counters
problem: The JEDEC PRAC+ABO (Per-Row Activation Counting + Alert-Back-Off) framework for DDR5 Rowhammer mitigation is only a specification framework, not a proven secure implementation; the prior Panopticon design that inspired it is shown to be insecure via a new 'Jailbreak' attack that causes 9x more activations than the configured threshold of 128. A provably secure, low-overhead DRAM-side Rowhammer mitigation using the PRAC+ABO framework does not yet exist.
method: MOAT (Mitigating Rowhammer with Dual Thresholds) uses per-row activation counters (PRAC) with two internal thresholds: ETH (Eligibility Threshold) for proactive mitigation during REF operations and ATH (ALERT Threshold) for triggering the ALERT-Back-Off reactive protocol. Instead of Panopticon's 8-entry per-bank queue (which loses counter information and enables Jailbreak), MOAT tracks only a single entry per bank via a Current Tracked Addr (CTA) register that always holds the row with the highest counter value, plus a Current Mitigated Addr (CMA) register, requiring only 7 bytes of SRAM per bank total. A safe counter-reset-on-refresh mechanism preserves counter integrity across refresh groups by copying boundary-row counters to 2-byte SRAM registers. The Ratchet attack analysis, exploiting the inter-ALERT activations permitted by JEDEC ABO specifications, establishes that MOAT with ATH=64 can safely tolerate a Rowhammer threshold of 99.

title: Enhancing CGRA Efficiency Through Aligned Compute and Communication Provisioning
problem: Existing CGRAs overprovision communication resources (routers consume 44% of power/area in spatio-temporal designs) relative to compute capabilities because each PE is paired with a full crossbar/router that handles peak congestion, resulting in low average communication utilization and wasteful programmability encoding.
method: Plaid proposes a hierarchical execution paradigm based on structural 'motifs' — recurring three-node subgraph patterns (fan-in, fan-out, unicast) in dataflow graphs (DFGs). The Plaid architecture replaces individual PE+router pairs with a Plaid Collective Unit (PCU): three ALUs share a single lightweight local router that handles all intra-motif communication internally, connected to a global router for inter-PCU communication. The Plaid compiler (built on the Morpher toolchain with simulated-annealing-based modulo scheduling) automatically identifies motifs in DFGs, generates a hierarchical DFG, and maps it onto the PCU array using flexible schedule templates that maximize resource utilization. Implemented in Verilog RTL at 22nm FDSOI targeting 100MHz; a 2x2 PCU array has 16 functional units (same as a 4x4 spatio-temporal CGRA).
